grammarRules.title: Indefinite Nominal Suffixation (-as) in Demonstrative Predications
grammarRules.explanation: In Brahui (especially the Sarawani dialect), indefinite singular nouns in demonstrative equational constructions are marked by attaching the enclitic indefinite suffix '-as' (orthographically represented as 'ءس' after a silent/vocalic heh or vowel-final loanword). When translating an indefinite equational statement (e.g., 'A test sentence' or 'This [is] a test sentence'), the proximate demonstrative 'دا' (dā) precedes the attributive modifier and the head noun inflected with '-as'.

examples.englishGloss: This is a test sentence / A test sentence

grammarRules.title: Vocative and Social Address Integration
grammarRules.explanation: In Brahui social interaction, standard Persian-derived greetings like 'Subh-e-bakhair' are considered incomplete when addressing a specific person. The language requires the addition of a noun or address term (such as 'sangt' for friend) to complete the social communicative act, reflecting the Dravidian emphasis on relational context.

grammarRules.title: Lexical Precision and Idiomatic Surface Reference in Standard Brahui
grammarRules.explanation: The correction reveals three critical linguistic nuances in Standard Brahui: 1) Idiomatic Surface: The 'surface' of water is idiomatically referred to as 'baj' (literally 'back') rather than 'tāl' (plate/flatness). 2) Active Participles: 'Flowing' is best captured by 'barokā' (coming/moving) rather than 'tolokā' (sitting/static). 3) Future Potentiality: To express 'might not be' or 'will not be', the future negative suffix '-ro' (mafro) is required instead of the simple present negative '-o' (mafo). Additionally, 'chaghli kanning' is the specific lexical choice for 'throwing' an object like a stone.

examples.englishGloss: Breaks the surface (back) of the water.

grammarRules.title: Strict SOV Word Order and Locative Case Suffix for Destination
grammarRules.explanation: Brahui is a Dravidian language requiring strict Subject-Object-Verb (SOV) word order. When expressing motion towards a destination (e.g., 'to Quetta'), the destination noun must be marked with the locative case suffix '-ṭī' (ٹی) and the inflected verb must be placed at the absolute end of the sentence.

grammarRules.title: Genitive / Possessive Suffix (-na / نا)
grammarRules.explanation: Possession is formed by affixing suffix -na directly to the stem. When used with 1st person pronoun "kan" (me), it forms "kan-na" (my/mine).

examples.correct: Kan-na pin Ahmad e / کنا پِن احمد ءِ

grammarRules.title: Dative/Purposive Case Suffix (-ki / کی) and Accusative (-e / ے)
grammarRules.explanation: Direct object receives -e when definite, while beneficiary/purpose receives -ki ("for the sake of / to").

grammarRules.title: Ablative Postposition Suffix (-ān / آن)
grammarRules.explanation: Movement away or origin is denoted by suffix -ān attached to location or person stems.

examples.correct: I shahr-ān bassuţ / ای شاہر آن بسٹ

grammarRules.title: Voiceless Lateral Fricative Orthography (ݪ / lh)
grammarRules.explanation: Brahui features the distinctive voiceless lateral fricative /ɬ/ preserved from Proto-Dravidian. In Perso-Arabic it is written as ݪ (lam with small v above) and in Latin Roman as "lh". Never substitute standard l or kh.

knowledgeDocuments.sampleSummary: This dictionary serves as a comprehensive lexicon documenting Brahui vocabulary through an English-to-Brahui translation framework, supplemented by a formal Romanization guide for Perso-Arabic scripts. Lexicon (A-Z) 15-275 -- 4 of 276 -- 4 The English Brahui Dictionary It is our endeavor to preserve and promote the Brahui language, literature and Brahui cultural heritage, and popularize it to as many people as possible. Local people as well as non-locals have done valuable works on Brahui language. Among them, apart from Ge

rmans, Russians and Indians, British Orientalists also have a big contribution. However, the step-motherly treatment of the Brahui language by its own people is not a new thing, but it has been going on for the last Khans of Kalat. As this dictionary, by Duncan Dixey, was sent to Khan Kalat for publishing, after it was written, the Brahui Khan excused himself from printing and publishing it and returned it, saying that they had no money to print this precious work to preserve. Even after that, there have been repeated attempts by Balochistani politicians to eliminate this language under a certain deliberate plan. One such attempt was made by the NAP government in 1972. Not leaving a box for Brahui language in the 1998 census is another example of this kind. -- 5 of 276 -- 5 Thus Brahui has always been neglected by the politicians of Balochistan. It was not easy for the British to establish a foothold in the state of Kalat without learning the Brahui language, because in order to rule here, they had to learn the language so as to deal with its people. Hence the British Raj also fixed a scholarship for its scholars learning Brahui. In the early days when the Christian missionaries ca

me here to preach Christianity, the religious Brahuis Muslim tried to thwart their mission in their own way and chose their language as a medium to awaken the Brahui masses. Durkhani School was such an institute defending Islam directly and promoting Brahui indirectly. However, since the Brahui Academy has been established, the work of preserving the heritage of Brahui language and literature has built up. Due to Khan of Kalat's unwillingness to publish it, the dictionary was handed over to the British Museum for archiving, from where it was brought by Dr. Abdul Rahman Brahui and given to Brahui Academy for publishing. The dictionary was first published in 1995 by the Brahui Academy but at that time it was printed in the same script (common English script) as written by Duncan Dixey, so it was difficult -- 6 of 276 -- 6 for a non-Brahui, let alone a native Brahui to know the correct pronunciation of the words it contained. But before printing the second edition it was assigned to, Dr. Hafeezullah Sarparra to review the dictionary and rectify the mistakes of 1st edition, Dr. hafeezullah Sarparra, due to his linguistic friendliness for Brahui, has painstakingly composed it in phoneti

c Roman script as well as written Perso-Arabic (Nastalik) transliteration of the words in it, so as to pave the way for not only native Brahuis but also non-Brahui researchers and students to be benefited from it. Some revisions and additions have also been made to the dictionary, it is hoped that it will now be a useful work for the people having interest in Brahui language. Dr. M. Salah ud Din Mengal Chairman Brahui Academy (R) Pakistan, Quetta -- 7 of 276 -- 7 English- Brahui Dictionary By Rev: A. DUNCAN DIXEY Rev: DUNCAN Dixey was attached with Mission Hospital Quetta. Here he learnt Brahui and compiled an English to Brahui Dictionary in 1920. Next year in 1921 it was typed and in December 1923 a copy was gifted to British Museum London. One typed copy was in the library of Dr. R. Holland which he borrowed me and I myself typed three copies of it. After Independence 1947, a copy was sent to Government of Pakistan Karachi which was forwarded to N.W.F.P Frontier (Khyber Pakhtunkhwa) for publication but it was returned as Brahui language was not spoken there. However, in 1921 it was completed and handed over to the Indian office library in the form of a manuscript, where it remained dumped for more than a half century. Dr. Abdul Rahman Brahui during his stay in England visited the said library and after weeks of strenuous search was able to unearth the manuscript. Prof. Aziz Mengal November 10th 1994. -- 11 of 276 -- 11 Preface (Reviewed Edition) Brahui is the oldest and the only Dravidian language of Pakistan. Henry Pottinger was first who introduced this language and its grammar to the West by his Travelogue “Travels in Sindh and Balochistan” in 1816. After that many writers and linguists analyzed and wrote on Brahui. During British rule over Kalat many English officers learnt and wrote on Brahui language, Duncan Dixey was also one of them, who during his job learnt Brahui here and started writing a dictionary in 1906 and after 15 years he succeeded to complete his book, but could not publish it then. About a half century after its completion this book was discovered by the pioneer of Brahui research Dr. Abdul Rahman Brahui and he handed over this unique work to Brahui academy for publishing. Its first edition was published in 1995, reviewed by Professor Aziz Mengal. Dictionary plays a vital role in preserving th

e cultural heritage of a language, I feel myself lucky and honored to be assigned the review of this important work done a century ago on Brahui language by a Non-Brahui. I have made some important revisions and additions in this book and tried to rectify the mistakes made in 1st edition also added the transliteration of words to make it easy to understand and well spell the Brahui words. -- 12 of 276 -- 12 No doubt, this precious lexical work of Brahui in English has much importance in the literary history of Brahui language. This book contains a number of borrowed words from Arabic and Persian languages which are commonly used in Brahui language, in spite of this, the Dictionary also preserves plentiful words of Brahui origin, some of which are archaic in Brahui language now. I am much thankful to the Brahui Academy specially the Chairman Dr. Salah ud Din Mengal for assigning me the important job of the review of this book to serve my mother tongue. I hope that the new and revised edition of this Dictionary would be much charitable for the students, scholars and teachers of Brahui language and also for the non-speakers to learn the lexicon of Brahui language. knowledgeDocuments.title: The Brahui Language: Vol I - Analytic Grammar (Denys Bray)
knowledgeDocuments.sampleSummary: Authoritative foundational treatise analyzing Brahui Dravidian roots, morphology, postpositional system, complex verbal affixes, reflexive pronouns, and comparative syntax with Dravidian languages.
chunks: Brahui Grammar Part I: Noun Declension. Nominative case has no suffix. Genitive affix is -na. Dative suffix is -e. Locative affixes are -āī (upon) and -ṭī (in, inside). Ablative is -ān (from). Associative suffix is -to (with). Purposive suffix is -ki (for).
Verbal Conjugation: Present-Future tense suffixes for Person: 1st Sing: -va/ -uţ; 2nd Sing: -sa / -us; 3rd Sing: -ik / -e; 1st Plur: -ona / -un; 2nd Plur: -ere / -ure; 3rd Plur: -ira / -o.

Negative conjugation: Formed by infusing -pa- or -fa- infix between the root and verbal inflectional termination. Example: karing (to do) -> kappara (I do not do), kunēk (he eats) -> kumpak (he does not eat).

knowledgeDocuments.title: Brahui Academy Comprehensive Lexicon & Terminology
knowledgeDocuments.sampleSummary: Over 8,000 core Brahui terms catalogued across Perso-Arabic and Roman scripts with English and Urdu definitions, etymology, and dialectical variations between Sarawani and Jhalawani.
chunks: Dictionary Extract A-B: Urā (noun) = House / Home (اردو: گھر). Dīr (noun) = Water (اردو: پانی). Elesh / Kūl (noun) = Bread / Food (اردو: روٹی / کھانا). Huch (noun) = Camel (اردو: اونٹ). Pīr (noun) = Rain (اردو: بارش). Khān (noun) = Eye (اردو: آنکھ).

Dictionary Extract M-P: Minatwār (adj) = Grateful / Thankful (اردو: شکرگزار). Mehrbāni (noun) = Kindness. Pin (noun) = Name (اردو: نام). Bā (noun) = Mouth (اردو: منہ). Kholum (noun) = Wheat (اردو: گندم).

Chapter 1: The Land of Balochistan.

Brahui is an ancient language spoken in Kalat and across the mountain valleys. The people have preserved their culture and language for generations.

Today, scholars and linguists study its Dravidian roots and unique grammar.

مرو، ماہرین علم او لسانیات اسہ ڈراوڑی ریشہ او تینا گونا اٹی ہیت کننگ تیا تحقیق کیر۔

Chapter 1: The Land of Balochistan.

Brahui is an ancient language spoken in Kalat and across the mountain valleys. The people have preserved their culture and language for generations.

Today, scholars and linguists study its Dravidian roots and unique grammar.
translationLogs.translatedText:
اولیکو بشخ: بلوچستان نا ڈغار۔

براہوئی اسہ مستین ءُ زبان اس ءِ ہرا قلات او مش نا درہ غاتیٹی ہیت کننگک۔ بندغاک پڑیا تیان تینا دود و ربیدگ او زبان ءِ سنبھال کرینو۔

اینو، عالم آک او لسانیات دان آک اینا دراوڑی بنیاد او بے مٹ گرائمر نا پٹ و پول ءِ کیرہ۔

translationLogs.sourceText: Brahui is a unique language spoken predominantly in Balochistan. Unlike its neighboring Indo-Aryan and Iranian languages, Brahui is historically classified as a Northern Dravidian language. Scholars continue to study its rich oral traditions and distinct grammatical features.
translationLogs.translatedText: براہوئی اسہ بے مٹ ءُ زبان اس ءِ ہرا گیشتر بلوچستان ٹی ہیت کننگک۔ تینا ہمسایہ انڈو آرین او ایرانی زبان تیان جتا، براہوئی تواریخی وڑاٹ اسہ قطبی دراوڑی زبان اس گوندنگک۔ زانتکار آک اونا گنجین زبانی روایت او جتا ءُ قواعدی صفت آتا مطالعہ ءِ برجا تخانو۔
